title: Managing spills of body fluid at work
audience: Cleaning staff who respond to spills in patient areas, clinics and shared spaces.
learningOutcomes: Describe the response to a spot, a small spill and a large spill.
Name the contents of a spill kit and explain why each item is disposable.
Say when a disinfectant belongs in the spill response and when it does not.

instruction.heading: Prompt action
instruction.body: Acting fast on a spot or a spill involving blood or bodily fluid is good infection control and matches workplace safety duties. Once the mess is up, clean the patch and apply any disinfectant the risk review requires. Leaving it lets microbes spread and exposes the next person.

instruction.heading: The method depends on setting and volume
instruction.body: In a patient area, a little spill can be dealt with using a detergent mix alone. A heavy release, such as a large quantity of vomit or urine, must first be boxed in. Visible solids are taken up with disposable absorbent paper, broken glass or sharps are lifted with forceps rather than fingers, and free liquid is soaked up using a granular clumping absorbent.

instruction.heading: Three levels of response
instruction.body: A spot gets dabbed up straight away with a damp rag or a paper towel, and the debris is binned. A small patch, roughly 10 cm across or less, is soaked up with absorbent material that goes into a sealed bag; the surface is then cleaned with warm detergent on a disposable cloth. A larger patch is covered in granular absorbent, scooped with a single-use scraper and pan into a watertight container, and mopped with detergent. The guideline's table also shows a hypochlorite wipe-down with drying for the small and large levels, but that step follows the risk assessment in “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals” and is not automatic.

instruction.heading: Disinfectant and alcohol
instruction.body: A disinfectant is not needed for every spill. Where one is required, particularly under transmission-based precautions, use a TGA-listed product with the right label claim. Alcohol is not used to clean spills. Soft furnishings are cleaned with detergent rather than hypochlorite.

instruction.heading: The spill kit
instruction.body: Each clinical room keeps a spill kit containing a scoop, a scraper, one-use gloves, a protective apron, a face mask, goggles, granular absorbent, clinical waste bags with ties, and detergent. Discarding every item after one use prevents carry-over between incidents.

procedure: Put on the protective equipment the procedure calls for before touching the spill.
Limit the spread: cover or confine the spill and keep people away from it.
For a spot, dab it up straight away with a damp rag or a paper towel, and bin the material.
For a small spill, wipe up with absorbent material, bag it, then clean with warm detergent using a disposable cloth.
For a large spill, cover it with absorbent clumping agent, scoop it into an impervious container, mop with detergent, then complete any disinfectant step the risk assessment requires.
Throw each used item into the proper bin, then wash your hands once the protective gear is off.
Record the time, the location, the type of substance and the steps taken, then report it to the supervisor.

workedExamples.situation: On a crowded children's ward, a child vomits a large amount onto the floor next to the bed. Visitors are close by and the nurses are tied up.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is your first action, and what is the order of the steps?
workedExamples.reasoning: Suit up, move onlookers away, and enclose the spill with granular absorbent. Shovel the material into a sealed, watertight container, scrub the patch using detergent, and use a disinfectant wipe only when the risk review says so. Wash hands, log when it happened and what the substance was, and tell the nurse in charge.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable utility gloves for spill work
Face mask and goggles where splashing may occur
Forceps for broken glass or sharps
Warm detergent mix and disposable cloths

commonErrors.error: Waiting for the spill to dry before cleaning it.
commonErrors.prevention: Act at once. Dried material is harder to lift and gives organisms more time to spread.

commonErrors.error: Picking up broken glass with fingers, even through gloves.
commonErrors.prevention: Lift broken glass or a sharp with forceps or a scraper, and treat the item as a sharp.

commonErrors.error: Using alcohol on a spill, or hypochlorite on upholstery, out of habit.
commonErrors.prevention: Alcohol is not used on spills; hypochlorite is used only as the risk assessment directs.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Wear the protective equipment the procedure requires for the whole task. Remove it correctly, and clean your hands straight afterwards.
Broken glass and sharps carry their own danger. Lift them with forceps or a scraper and drop them into a puncture-resistant container (see “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”).
Follow the label and the safety data sheet for hypochlorite, and ventilate the area.

qualityStandard: Spot, small and large spills are each managed by the stated steps.
Used materials are placed into the correct container and discarded.
The spill is recorded and reported to the supervisor.
documentationEvidence: Spill record with time, location, substance, volume and steps taken
summary: Clean spills promptly, with the protective equipment the procedure calls for.
Contain large spills first, remove visible matter, then mop with detergent.
A disinfectant pass is added according to risk, and alcohol stays off spills.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which step opens the response to a major release of bodily fluid?
options: Mop the whole floor immediately with detergent before anyone is told
Box in the spill and lift visible solids using disposable absorbent material.
Spray alcohol over the spill and leave it to dry on its own for an hour
Wait for the material to dry, then sweep it and then mop the floor with the same water

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is part of the guideline's spill kit contents?
options: A reusable mop that is shared between rooms and kept in the staff room
Single-use gloves, a protective apron and eye protection, with disposable parts.
A bottle of alcohol for disinfecting the spill and a cloth for the floor
A rag that is reused across all spills and kept clean in a bucket on the trolley

knowledgeChecks.question: When is a disinfectant part of a small spill response?
options: Straight away, on any spill, to be safe and before any containment is started
Only after the room is closed, because detergent alone is used and the door is kept shut
When a risk assessment backs it, using a TGA-listed product wherever disinfection is required.
Only when the spill is on soft furnishings and only in the afternoon of each day

sourceReferences: Australian Guidelines for Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, B1.4.3 (spills, Table B1.12, Recommendation 14, spill kit), B1.4.2 (soft furnishings); rights: not held by user; reworded (no copying)
